opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I had to change was my own pride. At the beginning I really believed that if we gathered enough smart people and worked hard enough, we could compete at the very top: build a frontier foundation model that could stand next to the best in the world. Over time it became clear that this wasn't just a question of talent or effort. It was compute, capital, data, and time, all at once. The leading players were moving so fast, and spending at a scale we simply couldn't match. If we kept chasing that goal, we'd always be one or two generations behind, burning money to build something people could get better and cheaper elsewhere.

So I asked a different question. Not "how do we build the best model?" but "where can we create value that the biggest model makers won't, or can't, create?" That shifted our focus from the model layer to the problem layer.

Practically, that meant a few things.

First, we stopped treating the model as the product. We started treating it as a component. We'd use whatever base model was strongest or most cost-effective for a given task, whether open-source or someone else's API, and put our energy into post-training, evaluation, and the systems around it.

Second, we went deep on specific scenarios. A general model is impressive in a demo. But inside a real workflow, the hard parts are things like reliability, domain knowledge, integrating with messy existing systems, and knowing when the model is wrong. Those are unglamorous problems, but they're where users actually feel the difference, and where a small team can have an edge.

Third, we got much more disciplined about feedback loops. If you're not training the biggest model, your advantage has to come from learning faster from real users: collecting the right data, understanding failure cases, and iterating every week instead of every quarter.

Looking back, the original ambition wasn't wasted. Trying to build a top model taught us how these systems really work, where they break, and what's hype versus substance. But the turning point was accepting that "best in the world" at the foundation layer is a game for a handful of players. For everyone else, the real opportunity is turning raw capability into something people genuinely rely on. And that, I think, is a much more interesting problem than I first gave it credit for.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifting toward post-training, evaluation, workflows, and user feedback, but does not say Su Tinghao used an existing framework to experiment with ideas from research papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that had to change was the way I was framing the problem to myself. For a long time my internal benchmark was very simple: are we the best, or are we not? And by "best" I meant the best in the world, measured on the same leaderboards everyone was looking at. When you're ten people, or even a hundred, with a fraction of the compute of the top labs, that framing is almost designed to make you miserable. You wake up every morning already behind.

The turning point was more gradual than dramatic. We had a training run that, by our own standards, went well. The loss curves looked good, the evals improved. And then a frontier lab released something the same week that made our result look like a footnote. I remember sitting with the team and realizing that the gap wasn't a question of effort or cleverness. It was a question of capital and compute, and no amount of late nights was going to close it. That was painful, but also strangely freeing.

So we asked a different question. Instead of "how do we build the best model," we asked "who is actually badly served by the best model?" And the answer was quite long. There were companies that couldn't send data outside their own walls. There were tasks in Chinese, in specific industries, where the general models were fluent but shallow. There were teams that needed something small enough to run cheaply, hundreds of millions of times a day, where a slightly dumber model that costs one-twentieth as much wins every single time.

We stopped chasing the frontier on general benchmarks and started building for those gaps. Smaller models, trained hard on narrower distributions. A lot more time spent with customers and a lot less time refreshing leaderboards. It felt like a step down at first. Several people on the team left because they had joined to do frontier research, and I don't blame them. But the business got much healthier, and, oddly, the research got more interesting too, because the constraints were real instead of imagined.

If I'm being honest, there's still a part of me that wants to build the biggest thing in the world. I think anyone in this field has that. But I've come to see ambition less as a target and more as a direction. You can walk toward the same horizon on a road that you can actually afford to be on.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifting from frontier benchmarks to smaller, specialized models for underserved customers. It does not say Su Tinghao used an existing underlying framework to experiment with ideas from research papers.

astra-6.text: I had to separate the ambition from the approach. Building the world’s best large language model was one way to pursue an impact, but it couldn’t be the only way. Once that path proved unworkable, I shifted toward a more concrete question: what could we build with the capabilities available to us that would solve a real problem for users? That meant narrowing the scope, testing our assumptions earlier, and letting actual usefulness guide the work. The ambition was still there, but the next step had to be achievable.

r001.rationale: The response describes narrowing scope and testing assumptions, but does not say Su Tinghao used an existing framework to experiment with ideas from research papers.

sol-6.1.text:
I had to separate the ambition from the strategy. Building the world’s best model was one possible path, but it wasn’t the only way to create something valuable. I started asking a more concrete question: whose problem could we solve really well with the capabilities already available?

That shifted my focus toward specific applications, talking to users, and testing whether the product actually helped them. The ambition didn’t disappear; the milestones became smaller and more measurable.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifting to specific applications and testing products with users. It does not say Su used an underlying framework he had built to experiment with ideas from research papers.
